name: Coating

origin.note: Infinite object coating appeared as an arXiv preprint in 2014; universal coating in [Derakhshandeh2017Coating].

summary: Particles must cover the surface of a fixed object as uniformly as possible.
statement: A fixed object (a connected set of lattice nodes) is surrounded by particles. They must arrange themselves into layers around the object, each layer filled before the next. **Time** in rounds; **moves** is the work.

primer.intro: Imagine a swarm of tiny robots asked to wrap a foreign object, like ants covering a crumb, one even layer at a time. The object is a connected set of nodes of the triangular grid that particles cannot enter; $n$ particles, connected to each other and to the object, sit around it. A particle sits on one node of an endless triangular grid and moves in two steps: it *expands* into an empty neighbouring node, briefly occupying both, then *contracts* into one of the two; so one expansion and one contraction move it by one node. They must arrange themselves into layers around the object: the first layer (the nodes touching the object) must be full before any particle sits in the second, and so on, with any extra particles in the last layer. In the standard version particles have constant memory, agree on clockwise (*chirality*), and may flip coins; we count *rounds* (stretches in which every particle acts at least once) and *work* (total moves).

ideas.title: Follow the leader around the object, layer by layer
ideas.idea:
The particles move in *handovers*: an expanded particle contracts and at the same moment pulls a neighbour into the node it vacates, so the chain never breaks.

1. Particles touching the object become *roots*; every other particle picks a neighbour closer to the object as its parent, so the swarm forms trees hanging off the object.
2. Roots walk clockwise around the object along the first layer; followers trail behind their parents by handovers.
3. A root that bumps into a particle that has already stopped stops too (it *retires*). A follower that still wants a spot sends a 'complaint' to a root with free space ahead, which then moves on and makes room.
4. A leader elected among the first-layer positions marks where the layer begins and ends. When the first layer is full, the next layer starts from that mark, and so on.
ideas.analysis: In the worst case the total work is $\Theta(n^2)$, which matches the lower bound below [Derakhshandeh2017Coating]. The running time is $O(n)$ rounds with high probability [Daymude2018Coating]; the coins are needed only for the leader election, and $O(n)$ is the best possible in the worst case. Particles with no memory and no messages can still coat a convex object with one layer, in $O(n^2)$ rounds [Navarra2023Coating].
ideas.why_it_matters: Spanning trees plus handovers became the standard way to move a whole swarm without ever disconnecting it.

ideas.title: A long tail of particles
ideas.idea: Put all $n$ particles in one straight line that touches the object only at its first particle, and let the object's surface be longer than $n$. The particle at distance $i$ from the object must end touching it, so it must travel about $i$ nodes, which takes about $2i$ moves. The last particle is at distance $n$, and an unkind scheduler may let it act only once per round.
ideas.analysis: The last particle needs about $n$ moves at one move per round, so every algorithm needs $\Omega(n)$ rounds in the worst case [Daymude2018Coating]. Adding the distances, $2(1+2+\dots+(n-1)) \approx n^2$, so every algorithm needs $\Omega(n^2)$ work [Derakhshandeh2017Coating]. Both bounds are matched by the algorithm above.
ideas.why_it_matters: It is the simplest example of the distance argument that underlies most lower bounds for programmable matter.

ideas.title: Local particles cannot see where the gap is
ideas.idea: Let the object be a long straight bar. The first layer is completely full except for one empty spot exactly in the middle below the bar, and one extra particle sits in the second layer exactly in the middle above it. Someone who sees everything solves it in a constant number of rounds: everybody on the first layer shifts one step around the bar, closing the gap, and the extra particle drops in. Local particles near the two ends of the bar cannot tell, within about $n/4$ rounds, which way the shift should go: information moves at most one node per round, and the situation looks the same from both ends.
ideas.analysis: So for about $n/4$ rounds the flows at the two ends are decided independently and by symmetry are equally likely to go either way; in the cases where they do not fit together, the layer is not yet correct. Hence any local algorithm is, on such inputs, about $n$ times slower than the best algorithm with global knowledge: a competitive ratio of $\Omega(n)$ [Daymude2018Coating] (Theorem 1).
ideas.why_it_matters: It shows that 'worst case over all inputs' is the right measure here, since comparing to the best possible run on each input is hopeless for local algorithms.

history: Coating was posed as a basic task for self-organising matter with **work** (moves) as the first measure [Derakhshandeh2017Coating]; rounds followed, with matching bounds [Daymude2018Coating]. Coating was later solved by silent, oblivious particles [Navarra2023Coating] and in 3D hybrid programmable matter [Kostitsyna2024Coating3D].

variants.title: Universal coating
variants.summary: Any object admitting a uniform coating is coated with optimal work, and in $\Theta(n)$ rounds with high probability.

preconditions: a line of $n$ particles attached to the object by one particle, the object's boundary longer than $n$

results.note: With high probability; randomisation enters only through the leader election.

variants.notes: Chirality is part of the model of both papers. In 3D hybrid programmable matter (one finite-automaton agent moving passive tiles), universal coating takes $O(n^2)$ steps, worst-case optimal against an agent with global knowledge [Kostitsyna2024Coating3D]. Checked against the full texts.

variants.title: SILBOT, chirality, deterministic
variants.summary: Silent oblivious particles with chirality coat a convex object with one layer, deterministically, in $O(n^2)$ rounds.

preconditions: informal argument before Theorem 4, not a theorem

assumes: exterior awareness: a particle can tell a hole from the outside

time.note: $\Theta(n^2)$ rounds; the lower bound is argued informally.

open: Multi-layer coating, which "seems unfeasible" in SILBOT [Navarra2023Coating].
variants.statement: Single-layer coating of a **convex** object, together with compaction of holes.

figure.caption: Coating, following [Derakhshandeh2017Coating]: particles touching the object (black) are roots, the others follow a parent closer to the object (forming trees). Roots walk clockwise along the first layer, one expansion and one contraction per node; when an expanded particle contracts, its child expands into the node it leaves (a handover), so the trees are pulled along without breaking. With as many particles as first-layer nodes, the walk ends when every node adjacent to the object is occupied (green); further particles would start the next layer.

frames.label: Start: roots touch the object; arrows point to parents
Roots walk clockwise along the first layer
Handover: the parent contracts, its child expands
Final: the first layer is filled
